heading: There is no experimentally warranted minutes-per-night figure
claim: The only systematic mapping of experimental homework-duration research found 11 K-12 publications, of which only 2 actually manipulated homework time — both primary-school — and it abandoned its dose-response meta-analysis for want of data.
terms: how many minutes per night optimal homework length duration experiment manipulated time no evidence dose response abandoned campbell
note: Guo et al. 2024, Campbell Systematic Reviews 20(3):e1431. The two studies are Koch 1965 (grade 6 arithmetic) and Dolean & Lervag 2021 (grade 2 writing). All included studies rated low quality; GRADE not attempted. Vote 3-0.

heading: There is no experimentally warranted minutes-per-night figure
claim: The Campbell review restricts its own conclusions to primary school and states that additional research is required to understand the impact of homework on secondary school students.
terms: secondary school students unknown restricted primary conclusions do not transfer adolescents teenagers
note: Verbatim from the review's conclusion. Vote 3-0.

heading: There is no experimentally warranted minutes-per-night figure
claim: GAP — no experimental evidence establishes an optimal daily assignment length at any age, and none at all for ages 12-15. Any minutes figure this repo adopts is a design choice, not an evidenced dose.
terms: how long should the assignment be twenty minutes thirty minutes design choice not evidence unknown optimal length
note: Underwrites build rule P2 in 06-build-rules.md.

heading: There is no experimentally warranted minutes-per-night figure
claim: REFUTED: that the only two experiments varying homework duration both favoured MORE time with no diminishing-returns point, and that this counts as evidence against a ceiling.
terms: more time is better no ceiling koch dolean lervag duration experiments favoured longer refuted
note: Refuted 0-3: two primary-school studies cannot establish a dose curve. Logged so it is not re-derived as support for a short-assignment rule. Neither claim nor negation asserted.

heading: The correlational dose curve, and where it flattens
claim: For junior high students achievement continued to improve with more homework until assignments lasted between 1 and 2 hours a night; past that it was no longer associated with higher achievement. For high school students the line kept climbing.
terms: one to two hours a night ceiling diminishing returns junior high middle school curve flattens plateau
note: Cooper, Robinson & Patall 2006, RER 76(1) p.9. The chart is Cooper's own 1989 nine-study synthesis carried forward; the 2006 pass added no new junior-high dose data and could not replicate the curve. Vote 3-0.

heading: The correlational dose curve, and where it flattens
claim: In a full-population Spanish sample the curve peaks at 90-100 min/day of total homework, but gains between 70 and 90 min barely reach 3% of an SD; the authors call 60 min/day reasonable and effective.
terms: sixty minutes a day optimum spanish ninety hundred minutes peak three percent standard deviation efficient
note: Fernandez-Alonso, Suarez-Alvarez & Muniz 2015, J Educ Psychol 107(4):1075-1085. n=7,725, mean age 13.78, 353 classes, 148 schools. Vote 3-0. CAUTION: the time measure is a four-option ordinal item, so 90-100 min is interpolated from four bins and is not a measured optimum.

heading: The correlational dose curve, and where it flattens
claim: The second Spanish sample's 60-70 min/day recommendation is a judgment call, not a modelled inflection: those models are linear three-level HLMs with no quadratic term.
terms: sixty seventy minutes recommendation judgment call not modelled no quadratic term linear hlm
note: N=26,543, mean age 14.4. Stated rationale is that schools assigning 120 min/day double the between-student spread in time spent (25 min to over 50 min). Do not cite as a measured optimum.

heading: The correlational dose curve, and where it flattens
claim: Every dose figure in this literature is TOTAL homework across all subjects, so it caps an English-only assignment and never sets one.
terms: total across all subjects not per subject cap does not set english share fraction budget
note: Underwrites build rule P5. No study in this base separates per-subject from total dose.

heading: The correlational dose curve, and where it flattens
claim: All dose-response figures are correlational and cross-sectional; the authors' own words are that the word effect must be understood as predictive effect.
terms: correlational cross sectional not causal predictive effect caveat self reported minutes

heading: The causal base is thin, immediate-only
claim: The whole causal warrant for assigning homework is five exogenous-intervention effect sizes: weighted d=.60 (95% CI .38/.82), falling to d=.48 after trim-and-fill, with three randomised studies at d=.53/.54.
terms: does homework work at all causal experiment effect size d point six trim and fill randomised
note: Cooper et al. 2006 pp.19-20. Vote 3-0. The effect loses significance entirely under an assumed ICC of .4.

heading: The causal base is thin, immediate-only
claim: The positive causal effect of homework has been tested and found ONLY on immediate unit tests, so no claim can be made about its causal effects on longer-term achievement.
terms: immediate unit test only no long term causal claim short term aligned content
note: Verbatim, Cooper et al. 2006. Vote 3-0. The unit test is aligned to the assignment's own content.

heading: The causal base is thin, immediate-only
claim: The two adolescent-age studies among Cooper's five causal effect sizes produced the two SMALLEST effects (.46 and .39), so d=.60 must not be transferred to a 13-14-year-old as a headline.
terms: adolescent smallest effects teenagers weaker do not transfer headline d point six
note: Vote 3-0.

heading: The causal base is thin, immediate-only
claim: A 2024 Campbell review pools 14 comparisons at g=0.45 (95% CI 0.24-0.66), from 10 articles spanning 1939-2021 with all but one predating 1996, I-squared 71.3%, all rated low quality.
terms: g point four five pooled campbell meta analysis homework versus none heterogeneity low quality old studies
note: Vote 2-1, so weaker than [V]. Component effects: arithmetic computation g=0.46, problem solving g=0.17, arithmetic concepts g=-0.02 (null). Practice-type outcomes benefit; conceptual understanding did not.

heading: The causal base is thin, immediate-only
claim: The Campbell review's planned subgroup analyses by gender, grade, subject and region were not feasible for lack of data, so all of them remain untested.
terms: subgroup analysis failed grade untested gender subject region insufficient data
note: Verbatim. Vote 3-0. Only one included study sampled 8th grade: Ewart Anderson 1946, n=58.

heading: Grade level moderates it
claim: The homework-achievement correlation is real only from about grade 7 up: secondary r=.25 fixed / .20 random against elementary r=-.04 / .05, the latter not different from zero under random error.
terms: secondary versus elementary correlation grade seven upward r point two five moderator age
note: Cooper et al. 2006 p.43. Q(1)=710.68 p<.0001 fixed; Q(1)=10.43 p<.002 random. Overall r=.24 fixed / .16 random across 69 correlations, 35 samples, 32 studies. Vote 3-0.

heading: Grade level moderates it
claim: The middle grades are not the secondary headline: Cooper's earlier meta of 50 correlational studies gives r=.07 for middle grades against r=.25 for high school.
terms: middle grades r point zero seven this learner's number not point two five thirteen fourteen year old
note: From Cooper 1989, 50 studies 1962-1987. This is the figure closest to a 13-14-year-old, and it is a correlation with self-reported TIME, which p01-5-* shows is the wrong lever.

heading: Grade level moderates it
claim: The grade moderator disappears when restricted to student respondents: secondary r=.19 versus elementary r=.22, Q(1)=0.57, ns — so part of the split reflects who reported the time.
terms: moderator fragile disappears student respondents who reported the time teacher parent report artefact
note: Cooper et al. 2006 pp.44-45. Also: 'strongest moderator' holds only under fixed-error assumptions; under the random-error model Cooper prefers, respondent type is a bigger moderator (Q=20.06 vs 10.43). Vote 3-0.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: At the individual-student level, time on homework predicts LOWER achievement once prior achievement and ability are controlled — replicated across four large samples in three countries.
terms: minutes spent negative predictor slower learners longer time is not progress do not display elapsed time
note: Spain N=26,543 mean age 14.4: individual betas Maths -0.050, Sciences -0.053, Spanish -0.055, Citizenship -0.055, all p<.001, while school-level betas are all positive 0.046-0.083. PISA-Germany n=24,273; TIMSS n=2,216 B=-.13; Berlin path model n=483 beta=-.14. Vote 3-0. Strongest and most transferable finding in this base.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: The sign of the homework-time coefficient REVERSES between levels of analysis: assigned volume at the school level is positive, time spent at the individual level is negative.
terms: sign reversal levels of analysis school level positive individual negative ecological
note: UNIT MISMATCH: the school-level figure is per assigned HOUR, the individual figure is a standardised beta per SD of individual time. This is a direction statement, never a magnitude comparison.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: The time finding replicates on a FOREIGN LANGUAGE: in 1,832 Swiss grade-8 students learning French, homework time was negatively related to achievement and to achievement gains however it was measured.
terms: swiss french as a foreign language grade eight replication diary self report vocabulary written work negative
note: Schnyder, Niggli, Cathomas, Trautwein & Ludtke 2006, 104 classes, three cantons, pre/post across grade 8. Vote 3-0. CITE AS REPORTED-IN Trautwein 2007 — it reaches us through a one-paragraph summary and carries no recoverable effect size.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: Homework EFFORT predicts achievement gains where time does not, and the two are separate constructs: effort beta=.16 on T2 grades against time beta=-.14, with effort and time correlated r=-.12.
terms: effort predicts gains conscientious completion not time uncorrelated separate construct what to measure
note: Trautwein 2007, Learning and Instruction 17:372-388, Study 3: 483 grade-8 students, mean age 13.45, 20 Berlin Gymnasium classes, controlling prior achievement, ability and gender. Vote 3-0.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: Trautwein's own conclusion: homework time is not a suitable indicator of the effort that students put into their homework.
terms: time is not a proxy for effort engagement conscientiousness verbatim conclusion
note: Verbatim, §5.3. Vote 3-0.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: The effort construct that predicts gains is a six-item SELF-REPORT (alpha .86/.84) anchored on 'I do my best in my homework' and 'I often copy homework from others' (reverse-scored).
terms: how effort was measured self report six items copy homework do my best collides with self assessment prohibition
note: This collides with ../ielts/09 E8 and §4.4, which forbid unanchored self-assessment. The collision is worked through in 06-build-rules.md §3 and P3.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: Reverse causation is the leading explanation for the negative time coefficient and is visible in the data: good T1 grades predicted LESS T2 homework time (beta=-.15).
terms: reverse causation weaker students take longer struggling slow not effort failing difficulty signature
note: A slow learner spending longer is the signature of difficulty, not of effort failing to pay off. This licenses 'do not measure minutes', never 'assign less'.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: The honest general statement is null-TO-negative, not negative: the time coefficient is significant on self-reported grades but null (beta=.03 ns) on a standardised test in the same study.
terms: null to negative not simply negative standardised test outcome differs qualification
note: Vote was 2-1 on the three-study replication claim; the dissent was that one of four outcome models was null rather than negative.

heading: Time is not the variable. Effort is
claim: Trautwein's scope warning limits transfer to a self-study site: the measures clearly targeted homework ASSIGNED BY THE TEACHER, extra study time was not included, and voluntary study time may behave differently.
terms: assigned by teacher not voluntary study extra time excluded scope limit self study website transfer

heading: Frequency over duration
claim: At the class level, more frequent homework assignments predicted higher achievement while the coefficient for homework TIME was not significant.
terms: short daily beats long weekly frequency versus duration how often not how long
note: Trautwein 2007 Study 2, German longitudinal TIMSS extension, N=2,216, 91 intact classes, grade 7 to 8, controlling prior achievement, cognitive ability, gender and school track. Vote 3-0. CAUTION: the .11 coefficient is UNSTANDARDISED (0.11 SD per one point on a 1-5 frequency scale), survives after 81% attenuation, mathematics only.

heading: Frequency over duration
claim: REFUTED: three parallel frequency-beats-quantity claims drawn from the two Spanish samples, including the quotable 'daily assignment beats sporadic by 15% of an SD'.
terms: fifteen percent of a standard deviation daily versus sporadic refuted do not use this figure spanish
note: Refuted 0-3. Neither claim nor negation asserted.

heading: Frequency over duration
claim: Frequency-over-duration is the best available design heuristic and not an established effect; it has never been tested on foreign-language homework, and must be marked [INF] wherever acted on.
terms: heuristic not established effect design choice short frequent sessions untested foreign language
note: Underwrites build rule P4. Only the TIME half of the finding replicates independently (De Jong 2000 NL; Schnyder 2006 CH; Muhlenbruck 2000 US).

heading: The one foreign-language dose benchmark
claim: A real-world benchmark for beginner foreign-language homework is ~12-17 expected minutes per day: grade-9 French I students were expected to do 12, 14 or 17 min/day depending on timetable.
terms: twelve fourteen seventeen minutes per day french beginner benchmark real world practice how much actually set
note: Wallinger 2000, Foreign Language Annals 33(5):483-496, Virginia, 60 CLASSES across 49 teachers. Vote 2-1. The figures are an arithmetic conversion of self-reported ANNUAL hours by an assumed 180-day year the author flags as not holding, and are internally inconsistent (17x5=85, not the stated 75). Descriptive practice, never a dose-response warrant.

heading: The one foreign-language dose benchmark
claim: A study varying both instructional time and expected homework found no significant difference in end-of-course speaking, writing, listening or reading performance.
terms: no difference four skills null result scheduling end of course test speaking writing listening reading
note: Vote 3-0. UNDERPOWERED NULL: reported secondhand from the author's prior work with no test statistics, no effect size and no power analysis, on a researcher-developed instrument, over a homework contrast of only ~13.7 h/year. Not evidence that homework quantity does not matter.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — foreign-language homework has essentially no evidence base: Cooper's synthesis of 32 studies and 69 correlations contained exactly ONE foreign-language study, omitted from the subject-matter moderator for having too few companions.
terms: no foreign language homework evidence one study only antonek dropped omitted subject matter moderator english
note: Vote 2-1 (dissent was scope wording, not substance). The single FL study is Antonek 1996, unpublished dissertation, n=89, r=+.26. Nearest proxy language arts was NULL (r=-.01 fixed, .01 random) while reading was positive (r=.21).

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — no study separates per-subject dose from total dose, so whether a 20-minute daily English assignment sits on the rising part of the curve or below its detection threshold cannot be answered.
terms: per subject versus total unknown fraction twenty minutes english detection threshold unanswerable

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP/REFUTED — the moderators a design would most want (purpose, choice, feedback, grading, parental involvement, frequency versus length) were not testable in the 2006 synthesis; the claim that they were is refuted.
terms: moderators untested purpose choice feedback grading what makes homework work characteristics
note: Only four moderator variables had enough studies. Refuted 0-3 as submitted.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — setting mismatch is total: every finding is teacher-assigned homework inside a school with a class and an accountability structure, and the one positive lever (school-level assigned volume) has no analogue in solo self-study from a static site.
terms: setting mismatch school class teacher accountability solo self study website no analogue

heading: Interleaving beat blocking, on adults
claim: Interleaved grammar practice beat blocked practice on a one-week delayed grammaticality-judgment test, d=0.64, with no significant advantage on the immediate test.
terms: interleaving versus blocking mixing grammar structures delayed retention d point six four one week
note: Nakata & Suzuki 2019, Modern Language Journal 103(3):629-647. 115 analysed of 151, Japanese EFL, aged 18-22, CEFR A2-B1, five structures, 50 MCQ items. F(2,107)=4.512 p=.013. Marked [S] not [V] because the effect is fragile: the omnibus ANCOVA showed NO significant main effect of Condition (F=2.122 p=.125) and only a marginal Time x Condition interaction (p=.064).

heading: Interleaving beat blocking, on adults
claim: In-session accuracy is not a proxy for retention: interleaving produced the WORST accuracy during training (77.0% vs 87.2%, d=0.83) and still beat blocking a week later.
terms: in session accuracy misleading desirable difficulty looks worse while doing it training performance
note: Vote 3-0. Underwrites build rule P6. The practice-phase percentages were not visible in an open copy of the paper.

heading: Interleaving beat blocking, on adults
claim: Learners could not tell the schedules apart, rating three arrangements of markedly different effectiveness as equally effective (5.31/5.61/5.63 on a 7-point scale; F=0.820, p=.443).
terms: learners cannot judge which practice works judgment of learning felt sense equally effective ratings
note: Vote 3-0. Ratings collected after the immediate posttest but BEFORE the delayed one, so no feedback channel existed to correct them. Underwrites build rule P7. The null is between-subjects and underpowered: it shows learners RATE schedules equally, not that they cannot discriminate.

heading: Why this is marked [S]
claim: Only 1 of 3 pairwise contrasts was significant and the paper's own second hypothesis (blocked-then-interleaved beats both) was NOT supported, so 'interleaving produced the best retention' overreaches.
terms: overreach safe statement pairwise contrasts hypothesis not supported what the study does not show
note: blocked vs increasing p=.339; increasing vs interleaved p=.667. The safe statement is that the schedule with the worst in-session accuracy beat blocking a week later. d=0.64 is ANCOVA-adjusted for three covariates, not a raw contrast. 24% post-hoc attrition.

heading: Why this is marked [S]
claim: The manipulation mixed five STRUCTURES inside one exercise format, and the outcome is an untimed receptive grammaticality-judgment test — so it is not evidence for mixing exercise types, task formats or skills, and not evidence about production.
terms: what interleaving means here structures not exercise types not skills receptive not productive scope

heading: The adolescent counter-finding
claim: Kim (2024, Language Learning) found the OPPOSITE direction for low-achieving adolescents on vocabulary: interleaving alone was an undesirable difficulty and blocked-then-interleaved won.
terms: adolescent counter finding opposite direction kim twenty twenty four low achieving vocabulary blocked first
note: Surfaced by a verifier. The target learner is exactly where the two studies disagree: an adolescent with low prior knowledge.

heading: The adolescent counter-finding
claim: GAP — whether to interleave or block for a 13-14-year-old at A2 is genuinely undetermined. One study says interleave (adults, receptive grammar); one says block first (adolescents, vocabulary). No mixing policy may be adopted from this evidence.
terms: should we mix or block undetermined cannot decide mixing policy blocked needs research
note: Underwrites build rule P13, marked [SPEC].

heading: Concrete day offsets
claim: REFUTED: Suzuki (2019)'s finding that four sessions spaced 3.3 days apart beat the same four spaced 7 days apart on oral production.
terms: twice a week beats once a week three point three days seven days oral production refuted day offsets
note: Refuted 0-3 for stripped hedges, a cherry-picked side of the result, and a provenance failure — the quoted sentence is not the cited paper's finding as claimed. Neither claim nor negation asserted.

heading: Concrete day offsets
claim: REFUTED: the Cepeda et al. (2008) rule that optimal inter-session interval is 8-43% of the retention interval.
terms: cepeda eight to forty three percent of retention interval optimal gap rule refuted generalisation
note: Refuted 0-3 as a generalisation, with more recent L2 grammar work contradicting its transfer. Neither claim nor negation asserted.

heading: Concrete day offsets
claim: GAP — nothing licenses 'review on day 2 and day 7' over any other schedule. The concrete-day-offset gap recorded in ../ielts/09 §2.1 stands unclosed after this pass.
terms: review ladder day offsets one three seven twenty one not evidenced gap stands engineering choice
note: Underwrites build rule P14. A ladder may still ship as an engineering choice, labelled one — see ../ielts/09 F4 and F5.

heading: The one authentic-classroom test
claim: In an authentic classroom, 66 primary-school students (Cantonese L1) studying 20 vocabulary items across three training episodes showed no significant difference between a 1-day and an 8-day review interval on a test four weeks later.
terms: rogers cheung one day versus eight day interval no difference classroom children vocabulary crossword
note: Rogers & Cheung 2020, SSLA 43(5):1138-1156. Sustained verbatim by four voters via the Crossref-deposited abstract. LIMITS: a null with no equivalence test (no TOST, no Bayes factor), no schedule-contrast effect size, and the population is primary-school children, younger than the target learner.

heading: The one authentic-classroom test
claim: REFUTED: the inference drawn from that null — that there is therefore no evidential basis for preferring a specific day offset. The study's own 2018 predecessor found a slight advantage for the 1-day interval.
terms: no basis for preferring offset inference refuted predecessor 2018 slight advantage equivalence not shown
note: A null in one replication does not establish equivalence across the window. The observation stands (p02-3-d); the generalisation does not.

heading: The one authentic-classroom test
claim: METHOD NOTE — the same study was sustained 3-0 in one pass and refuted 0-3 in another because the two panels were scoring DIFFERENT claims: the observation, and the generalisation drawn from it. Check what a verdict was about before treating it as a reversal.
terms: contradictory verdicts same study explained observation versus inference not a reversal check what was scored
note: Recorded in README.md §4 as well.

heading: The one authentic-classroom test
claim: The defensible statement is that no lab-derived optimal day offset is warranted for a school-age schedule — NOT that interval length is irrelevant. The counterweight is the L2 spacing meta-analysis finding shorter spacing less effective than longer on delayed posttests.
terms: interval length still matters err long delayed posttest counterweight kim webb what the null does not say
note: Counterweight is Kim & Webb 2022, already in ../ielts/09 §2.1 (98 effect sizes, 48 experiments, N=3,411).

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — optimal single-session length for adolescents. Nothing retrieved; the site's session length is an unevidenced design choice.
terms: how long should a session be session length adolescents unknown unevidenced

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — the daily-solo-plus-weekly-tutor architecture has no direct support. No study tests short daily solo sessions combined with a weekly consolidation session with a tutor.
terms: weekly consolidation session plus daily solo no evidence architecture week shape saturday
note: Restated in 05-tutoring.md §5 because it is as much a tutoring question as a scheduling one.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — whether interleaving transfers to productive work. The one L2 demonstration is a receptive judgment task; nothing establishes the effect for speaking or writing.
terms: productive work speaking writing interleaving transfer unknown receptive only

heading: Plan for attrition
claim: In a 6-month natural experiment on 601 Duolingo beginners, of seven candidate predictors only two survived into the best-fitting attrition model: L2 grit perseverance-of-effort and log(age).
terms: who keeps going dropout attrition predictors grit perseverance age duolingo app language learning
note: Sudina, Teimouri & Plonsky 2025, Learning and Individual Differences, doi 10.1016/j.lindif.2025.102704. Vote 3-0. Verified via OpenAlex after ScienceDirect returned 403. Single study, no replication located.

heading: Plan for attrition
claim: L2 motivation, grit consistency-of-interest, self-rated proficiency and measured pretest score did NOT meaningfully predict dropout — so motivational instrumentation aimed at making study more fun has no support here, and low proficiency is not a dropout risk signal.
terms: motivation does not predict dropout make it fun no support struggling learner not flight risk proficiency
note: Vote 3-0. Underwrites build rules P10 and P11. Exclusion from a model-selected fit is not identical to a null effect.

heading: Plan for attrition
claim: The actual attrition PERCENTAGE could not be retrieved (paywall), so this supports a qualitative rule and never a numeric figure; no odds ratios are obtainable.
terms: attrition rate number unknown paywall no percentage qualitative only no odds ratio
note: The sample is self-selecting adult Duolingo users on Spanish and French, and the log(age) term implies an adult spread. Nothing establishes any of it for a 13-14-year-old.

heading: Do not reward completion
claim: Expected tangible rewards undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation, and significantly more for children (57 studies, d=-0.39) than for college students (38 studies, d=-0.27); Qb(1)=4.18, p<.04.
terms: points badges prizes stickers undermine intrinsic motivation children worse than adults tangible rewards
note: Deci, Koestner & Ryan 1999, Psychological Bulletin 125(6):627-668. Vote 3-0. Underwrites build rule P9. The abstract hedges to 'tended to be more detrimental' while the moderator test clears p<.05.

heading: Do not reward completion
claim: The age caveat bites hard for a 13-14-year-old: in the paper's own words, most of the children were preschool or elementary students, but 6 studies used high school students.
terms: adolescents barely represented six high school studies age caveat preschool elementary upper bound
note: Six is an upper bound within that subset. Adolescents are thinly represented in the very cell the rule leans on.

heading: Do not reward completion
claim: REFUTED: the per-contingency effect sizes (engagement -0.40, completion -0.36, performance -0.28) and the verbal-praise claim that positive feedback enhances intrinsic motivation.
terms: per contingency figures refuted verbal praise enhances motivation not sustained do not quote
note: Per-contingency figures refuted 0-3; verbal praise not sustained (1-2), and its age split runs the other way, carried by college students. This base therefore contains NO warrant for any positive claim about praise.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — streaks specifically. The tangible-reward rule is from a 1999 laboratory meta-analysis; nothing was retrieved on streak mechanics as apps implement them, and a prizeless streak may not be a tangible reward at all.
terms: streaks daily streak counter mechanic unknown no evidence breaking a streak duolingo
note: Extending the tangible-reward rule to cover streaks is an inference, not a finding.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — reminders and notifications, implementation intentions, goal-setting for study behaviour, and habit-formation timelines. All four were explicit asks and returned no verifiable claim.
terms: reminders notifications implementation intentions goal setting habit formation how many days nothing retrieved
note: The widely repeated 'N days to form a habit' figures were not sourced, verified or admitted in any form.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — the L2 self-regulated-learning meta-analysis (g=0.72) was neither replicated nor refuted by this pass. Its marker stays [S] and its caveat — abstract and results disagree, publication bias detected — stays attached.
terms: self regulated learning meta analysis g point seven two publication bias unreplicated srl
note: Carried in ../ielts/09-design-principles.md §2.0. This pass was asked to find replications or refutations and found neither.

heading: TBLT is not available as a build rule
claim: The often-cited d=0.93 for task-based language teaching is a pooled effect over 52 heterogeneous TBLT IMPLEMENTATION studies, many single-group pre-post — not a head-to-head contrast with another method.
terms: tblt versus ppp task based language teaching d point nine three pooled not comparative
note: Bryfonski & McKay 2019, Language Teaching Research 23(5):603-632. Vote 2-1. Full text is closed access (Unpaywall is_oa false), so no CI, no heterogeneity statistic and no per-moderator significance is verifiable.

heading: TBLT is not available as a build rule
claim: The TBLT meta-analysis's moderators (program region, institution type, needs analysis, cycles of implementation) arrive with neither directions nor magnitudes, so they yield no design rule.
terms: moderators no direction no magnitude unusable do not cite d point nine three as warrant
note: Vote 3-0. Underwrites the blocked-list entry in 06 §2. The field's principal published criticism (Harris & Leeming 2022, IRAL) faults the meta-analysis for including studies lacking control groups or using different pre/post tests.

heading: TBLT is not available as a build rule
claim: REFUTED: three stronger claims — that no warranted TBLT effect size exists at all, that the comparative subset was wholly unfit for purpose, and that the obstacle is definitional (no consistent definition of 'a task').
terms: no warrant exists at all definitional problem what counts as a task refuted stronger claims
note: Each refuted 0-3. The absence of a usable warrant is established; the stronger claim that the literature is worthless is not.

heading: The one head-to-head result
claim: The one head-to-head study found the answer depends on when you measure: PPP better for immediate task performance, TBLT better for longer-term development.
terms: head to head split ppp immediate tblt long term depends when you measure harris leeming
note: Harris & Leeming 2022, IRAL, doi 10.1515/iral-2022-0082. Single study. Rhymes with the pattern in 02 §1: the arrangement that looks better in-session is not the one that looks better later.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — extensive LISTENING has no established evidence base here: no effect size, no meta-analysis. Do not assume extensive reading's well-replicated result (d approx 0.41-0.46) transfers by symmetry.
terms: extensive listening effect size unknown does not inherit from extensive reading symmetry assumption
note: The most conspicuous absence in this base. Extensive reading is the best-replicated intervention in ../ielts/09 §2.2; nothing comparable was established for listening.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — explicit versus implicit grammar instruction for adolescent EFL learners, input flood, visual input enhancement, dictogloss, the output hypothesis, and the ordering of receptive versus productive work inside a lesson. All explicit asks; none survived verification.
terms: explicit implicit grammar input flood enhancement dictogloss output hypothesis receptive productive ordering lesson shape
note: A visual-input-enhancement meta-analysis was fetched and its claims extracted, but none was sustained. These are research targets, not settled questions.

heading: Tutor type
claim: Tutoring effects by tutor type: teacher 0.50, paraprofessional 0.40, non-professional 0.21, parent 0.23 SD — so an untrained family tutor sits at the low end, not at the 0.37 pooled headline.
terms: uncle family tutor untrained non professional parent effect size versus teacher paraprofessional saturday
note: Nickow, Oreopoulos & Quan 2020, NBER w27476, Table 3A; peer-reviewed successor in AERJ 2024. 96 studies, 732 estimates. Vote 3-0. The parent cell is the table's weakest: 11 studies, p<.10, 95% CI roughly 0.01-0.45. NO L2 or foreign-language studies in the corpus at all.

heading: Tutor type
claim: REFUTED: the bare '0.37 SD' pooled tutoring effect used as the benchmark a weekly family session should clear.
terms: point three seven benchmark refuted pooled average misuse tutoring headline
note: Refuted 0-3. It is a pooled average across tutor types, settings and grades; the relevant cells are 0.21 and 0.23.

heading: Effects attenuate with grade
claim: Tutoring effects tend to be strongest in the earliest grades; the grades 6-11 pooled estimate is 0.16, but only 7% of interventions involve grade 6 or above and no reliable standard error can be calculated for that band.
terms: grade attenuation older students weaker sixth grade and up seven percent extrapolated no standard error
note: Vote 2-1. Attenuation is measured through grade 5 and extrapolated beyond it, and is 'explained entirely by literacy programs' — mathematics shows the reverse. The age band this learner is in is where this literature is thinnest.

heading: Parental homework involvement
claim: Parental homework involvement shows an overall WEAK NEGATIVE relationship with achievement: r=-0.064, p<0.001, across 28 studies, 32 samples, 252 effect sizes and 378,222 participants.
terms: parents helping with homework negative correlation should the daily work need an adult supervision
note: Xu, Guo, Feng, Ma, Zhang, Nunez & Fan 2024, Psicothema 36(1):1-14, doi 10.7334/psicothema2023.92. Vote 3-0. Underwrites build rule P8.

heading: Parental homework involvement
claim: SCOPE: that finding measures a parent supervising or assisting with DAILY HOMEWORK, not a scheduled weekly one-to-one session. It bears on whether daily assignments should require adult help (no) and not on whether a weekly tutor session is worthwhile.
terms: scope note daily supervision versus weekly session different question does not answer saturday hour
note: Correlational, and the dominant explanation is reverse causation: parents intervene more when a child is already struggling. Licenses 'no positive association to lean on', never 'parent help harms'.

heading: The refuted autonomy-support moderator
claim: REFUTED but unresolved — that only AUTONOMY SUPPORT relates positively to achievement (r=0.164), with content support, parental control/monitoring and involvement frequency all null.
terms: autonomy support versus content support moderator refuted needs re verification most design relevant
note: Voted down 0-3 despite appearing in the meta-analysis's own moderator decomposition. It would distinguish a tutor who supports independence from one who supplies answers — the actual design question. TREAT AS UNRESOLVED RATHER THAN FALSE. Highest-value target for the next research pass.

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — what a fluent-but-untrained adult should do with 60 minutes. The tutoring literature answers who tutors and how much, and answers neither what they should do nor what they should do in a language they speak but were never trained to teach.
terms: what should the saturday hour contain what to do with the tutor session unknown untrained fluent adult

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — whether structured materials or scripting raises a non-professional tutor toward the paraprofessional 0.40. This is the one lever a static site could actually pull, and nothing establishes that pulling it works.
terms: prepared session script structured materials for the tutor raise effect unknown lever

heading: What this file does not establish
claim: GAP — productive and speaking practice for a learner with no daily conversation partner. Nothing retrieved, and this repo separately forbids Speaking rubrics and Speaking feedback tooling — so there is neither evidence for what to do nor permission to score it.
terms: speaking practice no partner productive practice alone conversation partner forbidden speaking rubric
note: The Speaking prohibition is in ../ielts/README.md §5.

claim: Elapsed time is never displayed, recorded as progress, or used to rank sessions.

note: Finding 01 §5 [V 3-0]; rule [INF]. Fails if: a 'time studied this week' counter, a minutes-based streak, or anything sorted by duration.

heading: The checklist — P3
claim: The progress signal is effort-shaped and objectively anchored — attempts committed, tasks completed as real attempts, items produced rather than picked — never elapsed time and never the learner's self-rating.

note: Finding 01 §5 [V 3-0] plus ../ielts/09 E8 and §4.4 [S]; rule [INF]. The collision between the effort finding and the self-assessment prohibition is worked through in 06 §3.

heading: What is blocked
claim: BLOCKED LIST — a mixing/interleaving policy; any evidenced review-day ladder; a streak mechanic; a prepared script for the Saturday session; any extensive-listening programme warranted by analogy to extensive reading; citing d=0.93 for TBLT; any autonomy-support rule for the tutor. 'Blocked' means do not build it yet, never it cannot work.
terms: blocked list what not to build yet unblocking conditions seven items
note: Each entry names what would unblock it. Modelled on ../ielts/09 §7.1.

heading: The collision at P3, worked through
claim: The effort finding and this repo's self-assessment prohibition do not actually conflict: the research needed to MEASURE effort and used a self-report; this site does not need to measure effort, it needs to not measure time and to record something that is not time.
terms: collision resolved effort self report versus e8 prohibition what to record instead
note: The three behavioural signals already in the repo: an attempt was committed (:::task), a retake was taken, an item was produced rather than picked (review queue ranking).

heading: The collision at P3, worked through
claim: GAP — whether those three behavioural signals (committed attempt, retake, produced-not-picked) actually stand in for the effort construct that predicted gains is unestablished. Nothing validates them against it.
terms: do the proxies work substitution not validated effort construct unestablished
note: P3 says what to record and does not claim the substitution has been shown to work.

heading: What this base is not
claim: This base carries no IELTS claims: nothing here may appear in a :::bridge, and check_ielts.py resolves citations against ../ielts/ only. It is not a curriculum, does not license a weekly schedule, and never reaches a page.
terms: not for bridge directives no ielts claims not a curriculum never on the page separate base

heading: Provenance and method note
claim: METHOD NOTE — an absence reported by a fan-out research process is only evidence of absence if the search was actually run. The first pass reported three of five angles as finding nothing; they had never been put to a panel, because a global top-N ranking let one angle sweep every verification slot.
terms: never tested read as found nothing budget starvation global ranking per angle floor research process failure
note: The fix was a per-angle verification floor. The same failure would be invisible in any future pass that did not check.

heading: Verification hygiene
claim: Several verifications in this pass ran with an exhausted web-search budget and could interrogate only the primary source, not hunt for contradicting literature — so 'no contradicting evidence found' is weaker than the vote counts suggest for most of 01 §2-§6, 02 §1, 04 §1 and 05 §1-§3.
terms: search budget exhausted no contradiction hunting weaker than vote suggests verification hygiene

heading: Verification hygiene
claim: Five surviving claims were found materially wrong as first stated and corrected before entry: an unstandardised coefficient labelled standardised; '60 teachers' that is 60 classes; an overreaching 'interleaving produced the best retention'; a secondhand Swiss summary carrying no recoverable statistics; and a claimed attrition rate that does not exist in the retrievable text.
terms: corrections errors found in verification mislabelled figures travel with the findings

heading: Read the limits first
claim: The population is wrong in at least one dimension for every finding in this base: none Vietnamese, none a self-study website, two thin exceptions aside none a foreign language, and the 13-14 band is where this literature is thinnest. Every build rule is therefore [INF] even where its finding is [V 3-0].
terms: population mismatch extrapolation vietnamese self study website foreign language thinnest band inf
note: The standing marker rule for this base.
